planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in shade to partial shade; Annelise colors best with a little bright, indirect light but still scorches in hot direct sun.

directions: Annelise is a bold gold-variegated sport of Japanese aralia, its huge, deeply lobed, leathery leaves smudged with irregular patches of golden-yellow and lime green rather than the crisp white margin of 'Variegata' or the fine speckling of 'Spider's Web'. It stays a bit more compact and slower-growing than plain green Fatsia japonica, which makes it well suited to large containers as well as shaded borders. Small rounded clusters of cream flowers appear in autumn on established plants, often followed by black berries, though the plant earns its keep almost entirely on foliage. Grow it in humus-rich, moisture-retentive soil sheltered from harsh wind and hot midday sun, and strip out any all-green reverted shoots as soon as they appear to keep the variegation strong.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Moseri tolerates more cold and wind than typical seed-grown Fatsia japonica, making it a good choice near the colder edge of its range.

directions: Moseri is an all-green selection of Japanese aralia prized for its dense, compact habit and more pronounced, finely divided leaf lobes compared to the looser, seed-grown species. This clone forms a rounder, tidier crown than typical fatsia and is noticeably more resistant to cold and wind damage, a trait that has made it popular with European growers even though it remains uncommon in American nurseries. Clusters of white flowers on pale stems appear from autumn into winter, followed by black berries that persist into spring. Site it in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, sheltered from the harshest winter exposure, and prune only to remove damaged or overly long stems.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in a sheltered, frost-free shade bed with moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil.

directions: Green Fingers is a striking selection of the Formosan aralia whose leaves are cut nearly to the base into narrow, widely spaced, finger-like lobes, giving the plant a much more dissected, almost skeletal texture than the broad-lobed leaves of common Fatsia japonica. It keeps the same architectural, jungle-like presence that makes fatsia valuable in deep shade, but its lacy silhouette reads as a distinct accent among the bolder foliage of hostas and other shade perennials. Rounded clusters of small white flowers appear in autumn on mature wood, followed by black fruit. Grow it in a sheltered, frost-free shade bed with moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil, and protect it from cold wind and hard freezes at the colder edge of its range.

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil in shade to partial shade; Pia's shortened internodes give it a denser, bushier habit than the species, so it needs less staking to hold an upright shape.

directions: Pia is a compact sport of the Fatsia-ivy hybrid, bearing glossy, palmately lobed leaves about half the size of the species with distinctly wavy, undulating margins. Its shortened internodes give the plant a denser, bushier habit than typical Fatshedera lizei, which otherwise sprawls or climbs if left untied. Small globose clusters of white flowers can appear on mature growth in autumn, though the plant is grown chiefly for its crimped, textural foliage. Grow it in humus-rich, well-drained soil in shade to partial shade, sheltered from harsh wind and hot afternoon sun, and pinch growing tips occasionally to encourage even bushiness.
